item.text: {"question_id":"2B.7","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s government participated in the Nairobi and Luanda peace processes and backed formal ceasefire, withdrawal, monitoring, verification, disarmament, and cantonment mechanisms (BATCH-0027-E010; BATCH-0027-E013; BATCH-0021-E001; BATCH-0015-E002). Early implementation produced limited positive effects: M23 withdrawals in January allowed some roads to reopen and displaced people to begin returning, while ceasefire arrangements reduced hostilities for several months (BATCH-0023-E010; BATCH-0018-E002; BATCH-0027-E006). However, the record does not establish that Tshisekedi personally ensured compliance or that the government’s engagement was sincere beyond documented participation and commitments. Kinshasa rejected political dialogue with M23, adopted a hardline position toward the EAC process, and the EAC mandate ended after the government judged that it had not achieved expected results (BATCH-0011-E017; BATCH-0011-E016). M23 did not fully withdraw, the ceasefire broke down in October, violence and territorial control increased, and late-year fighting caused substantial displacement (BATCH-0004-E001; BATCH-0027-E006; BATCH-0013-E014). The November MONUSCO disengagement plan was a formal planning milestone, not demonstrated settlement implementation or a durable outcome within 2023; Tshisekedi had also requested an accelerated withdrawal, with its effects not yet established (BATCH-0010-E007; BATCH-0010-E017). Overall, the evidence shows documented but contested peace-process participation, some temporary ceasefire and withdrawal gains, incomplete compliance and implementation, and no durable settlement by the end of the period.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0027-E010","BATCH-0027-E013","BATCH-0021-E001","BATCH-0015-E002","BATCH-0023-E010","BATCH-0018-E002","BATCH-0027-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0011-E017","BATCH-0011-E016","BATCH-0004-E001","BATCH-0027-E006","BATCH-0013-E014","BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0010-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence documents government participation, plans, and attributed policy positions more clearly than personal negotiation, compliance, enforcement, or causal responsibility for breakdowns.","Several adverse claims involve competing regional interpretations, allegations, or multi-actor conflict dynamics; the evidence does not isolate Tshisekedi’s responsibility for M23 conduct, ceasefire failure, EAC shortcomings, or humanitarian deterioration.","The MONUSCO disengagement plan and accelerated withdrawal decision occurred late in 2023, so implementation and durability were not observable within the period.","The evidence does not provide a complete record of all ceasefire obligations, confidence-building measures, or lawful settlement compliance by each party."],"corrections_made":["Removed the unsupported characterization of the engagement as 'genuine'; the answer now describes documented participation and commitments without inferring sincerity.","Added the material positive evidence that early withdrawals reopened roads, enabled limited returns, and that ceasefires reduced hostilities for several months.","Reduced the weight of the MONUSCO plan by treating it as late-period planning rather than completed settlement implementation or demonstrated durable impact.","Qualified attribution for ceasefire breakdown, EAC failure, M23 noncompliance, and worsening humanitarian outcomes."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A fuller ledger could clarify Tshisekedi’s personal role in negotiating and enforcing each agreement, including the specific March/April ceasefire arrangements.","Additional independent records could establish whether Kinshasa implemented the Nairobi commitments on humanitarian access, P-DDRCS, monitoring, and dialogue, and whether alternative diplomatic options were realistically available.","Later outcome evidence would be needed to assess whether the MONUSCO transition plan or any ceasefire mechanisms became durable."]}
